articles.title: Embeddings and vector search explained: cosine similarity, HNSW and when to add keyword search
articles.excerpt: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that a model produces for a piece of text, such that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors. Vector search finds the stored vectors closest to a que…
articles.body: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that a model produces for a piece of text, such that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors . Vector search finds the stored vectors closest to a query's vector, usually by cosine similarity . Comparing against every vector is too slow at scale, so databases use approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes such as HNSW , trading a little recall for a lot of speed. Embeddings are weak at exact terms , such as names, IDs and error codes, so most production RAG systems add keyword search ( BM25 ) and combine the two: hybrid search . What is an embedding? An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector, often 384 to 3,072 numbers.

articles.title: A requirement ledger for coding agent handoffs
articles.excerpt: Your coding agent has a green test run and a finished patch. A reviewer then finds a compatibility requirement in an older discussion that the patch missed. Track each requirement from its source to a…
articles.body: Your coding agent has a green test run and a finished patch. A reviewer then finds a compatibility requirement in an older discussion that the patch missed. Track each requirement from its source to a specific verification result so the handoff exposes that gap. TokenWave AI's SWE-CoWork paper gives this problem a useful shape. The benchmark puts coding agents in simulated organizations around 101 real repositories. Agents start with a short handoff and must find requirements in workplace records and conversations with simulated colleagues, implement the changes, and submit a handoff. The researchers evaluate the result with private executable tests. The assignments are substantial: the paper reports a median of six accountable owners, 60 files and 32 verifier test nodes per task.

articles.title: The Attacker Never Broke In. They Logged In for 11 Days. published: false tags: security, cybersecurity, devops, iam
articles.excerpt: This is a composite, anonymised case from Book 5 of our IAM Architecture Series. The details are changed, but the pattern isn't rare. Day 0. A mid-sized insurer runs one shared domain admin account ac…
articles.body: This is a composite, anonymised case from Book 5 of our IAM Architecture Series. The details are changed, but the pattern isn't rare. The timeline Day 0. A mid-sized insurer runs one shared domain admin account across 40 servers. The password sits in a team wiki because "the vault is slow." It has no owner, isn't in the vault, and hasn't been reviewed in 14 months. A contractor gets phished at 14:02, and the attacker finds the wiki page within an hour. Then they log in from a device the company has never seen. No alert fires, because a domain admin logging in is normal. Day 1. A new service account appears with domain-wide rights: svc-backup-audit . No ticket. No approval. It isn't in the inventory, because discovery last ran as a one-time project nine months earlier. Day 2.

articles.title: Why we didn't add a token_delivery parameter
articles.excerpt: Mobile apps broke our refresh tokens, and the obvious fix would have broken everything else. Canopy issues a refresh token when someone signs in. In a browser it goes into an httpOnly cookie, which is…
articles.body: Mobile apps broke our refresh tokens, and the obvious fix would have broken everything else. Canopy issues a refresh token when someone signs in. In a browser it goes into an httpOnly cookie, which is the right answer there for one specific reason: page JavaScript cannot read it. A script injected into a customer's site cannot steal what the browser refuses to hand over. An installed phone app has none of that. No cookie jar, nothing re-sending credentials in the background. So the token has to come back in the response body, and the app stores it in the Keychain or the Keystore. Which means the API needs to know which kind of client is asking. The obvious way to tell it is a parameter on the request: token_delivery: "cookie" | "body" , defaulting to cookie .

articles.title: Kubernetes DiskPressure: How to Find Which Pod Is Eating Your Node's Disk (Bottlerocket Included)
articles.excerpt: Your pager goes off. A pod got evicted. You run kubectl describe node and there it is: DiskPressure=True. So you do what everyone does. You open a shell on the node and run df -h. It says 90% full. Yo…
articles.body: Your pager goes off. A pod got evicted. You run kubectl describe node and there it is: DiskPressure=True . So you do what everyone does. You open a shell on the node and run df -h . It says 90% full. You run du -sh /* and add it up. It says 40%. Where did the other half of the disk go? If your nodes run Bottlerocket, it gets worse. There is no SSH, no package manager, and no crictl on the host. The usual playbook does not even start. This post walks through a method that works on any Kubernetes node, and a read-only script that does the whole investigation for you. It tells you which namespace, pod and container is using the disk, what is growing right now, and what already got evicted in the past. It works even when the node is healthy today.

articles.title: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966
articles.excerpt: It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.
articles.body: Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky. At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history. It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

articles.excerpt: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.
articles.body: More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye. That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town. The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Original Annotated Milky Way versus Aurora Explanation: Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky? No, but it sure looks like it!
